opus-5.5.text:
I think the core appeal is that it lets you avoid having to win an argument about the future before you act. There's a huge range of views on how dangerous AI will be and when. Some people think catastrophic risks are imminent; others think they're decades away or overblown. If your safety plan requires everyone to agree on a forecast first, you're stuck.

Tying precautions to capability evaluations sidesteps a lot of that. The commitment basically says: we don't need to agree right now on whether models will be able to, say, meaningfully help someone build a bioweapon. What we can agree on is that *if* a model can do that, we'd need much stronger protections in place. Then you build tests that check for those capabilities, and the precautions kick in when the evidence shows up. Someone who's skeptical can sign on because they expect the expensive measures won't be triggered for a long time. Someone who's worried can sign on because there's a concrete tripwire.

It also gets the costs roughly right. Very strict security and deployment restrictions are expensive. They slow you down and make products worse. Imposing all of that on today's models, which mostly aren't capable of catastrophic harm, would be costly and hard to justify, and a company that did it unilaterally would probably just fall behind. Doing nothing until it's obviously too late is the opposite failure. Scaling precautions with demonstrated capability puts the burden where the risk actually is.

And I think it's useful for building toward broader norms or regulation. "Here's a test, here's a threshold, here's what you must do if you cross it" is something you can write down, audit, and potentially have other labs or governments adopt. It's much more concrete than a general promise to be careful.

It isn't perfect. Evaluations can miss capabilities, especially things that only show up with clever prompting, fine-tuning, or better scaffolding later on. So you need safety margins: you test for warning signs a bit below the level you're truly worried about, and you keep improving the evals. But as a framework for making real commitments under deep uncertainty, I think it's one of the better tools we have.

r001.rationale: It says skeptics can agree to precautions triggered by demonstrated capabilities, since they expect costly measures will not be needed for a long time.

r002.rationale: It says precautions should scale with demonstrated capability and activate when evaluations show risky abilities, placing costs where the risk is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind what we call the Responsible Scaling Policy is that you want to match the level of precaution to the level of risk. And the honest truth is that today's models, while they're impressive, probably aren't capable of causing catastrophic harm. So if you impose really extreme restrictions on them now, you're paying a big cost for not much safety benefit, and you probably won't be able to sustain those restrictions anyway.

The other thing I like about tying it to evaluations is that it turns a lot of vague disagreement into something concrete. People argue endlessly about whether AI is dangerous, and a lot of that comes down to different intuitions about what future models will be able to do. If instead you say, "Here is a specific capability we're worried about, here's the test we'll run, and if the model passes that test, here are the safeguards we commit to having in place before we go further," then you've made a falsifiable claim. Either the model can do the thing or it can't, and either you've put the protections in place or you haven't.

And it lets you make commitments ahead of time, when you're not under competitive pressure. It's a lot easier to say "we won't deploy a model that can meaningfully help someone build a bioweapon unless we have these mitigations" before you've spent an enormous amount on training it. Once the model exists and the incentives are pushing you to ship, that's exactly the moment you don't want to be deciding what counts as safe enough.

The flip side, and I want to be candid about this, is that it puts a lot of weight on the evaluations being good. If your evals miss a capability, or if the model has it but doesn't show it under testing, then the whole framework is giving you false confidence. So you have to build in margin, test for things before you expect the model to have them, and keep updating as you learn more. It's not a complete solution. But I think it's the most reasonable way to actually scale precautions with the risk rather than guessing.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations can make disagreements about AI danger more concrete, but it does not identify this as a way to build support among people skeptical of catastrophic risk.

r002.rationale: It says precautions should match the level of risk and describes putting safeguards in place when a model passes a capability test, tying precautions to demonstrated danger.

astra-6.text:
I think the main advantage is that it ties the precautions to evidence about the risk. There’s a lot of uncertainty about how quickly AI will improve and when particular capabilities will appear. If we base everything on a date, or on how much compute went into training a model, we could end up requiring precautions too early or introducing them too late.

Evaluations give us a way to ask more directly: can this model do something that would make it dangerous? Could it substantially help someone carry out a cyberattack, for example? If it can, that’s a reason to require stronger security and restrictions on deployment.

You’d want to agree on those responses in advance, so you’re not deciding what counts as acceptable risk at the moment you have a commercially valuable model ready to release. And you need a margin of safety: failing to elicit a dangerous capability doesn’t prove it isn’t there. But I think evaluations provide a useful basis for making precautions more demanding as the evidence of danger increases.

r001.rationale: The response explains that evaluations connect precautions to evidence of danger, but does not say this would build support among people skeptical that AI could pose catastrophic risks.

r002.rationale: It says evaluations help determine whether a model can do something dangerous and that stronger precautions should follow when evidence of danger increases, linking precautions to demonstrated risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that we’re quite uncertain about how quickly AI will improve, and which capabilities will create serious risks. So it makes sense to connect precautions to evidence about what a model can actually do. If it can help someone carry out a dangerous task, or act autonomously in ways that are difficult to control, that should trigger stronger safeguards.

That also gives developers a concrete target: before you build or deploy a system with those capabilities, you need to have the relevant protections in place. You can prepare those protections ahead of time, even if you don’t know exactly when you’ll need them.

The important caveat is that evaluations are imperfect. Failing to elicit a dangerous capability doesn’t prove it isn’t there. So I’d want a margin of safety, and I wouldn’t treat evaluations as the only evidence that matters. But they give us a way to make precautions responsive to the risk, rather than relying entirely on guesses about dates or model size.

r001.rationale: The response ties precautions to evaluations, but does not say this approach could build support among people skeptical of catastrophic AI risks.

r002.rationale: It says stronger safeguards should follow when a model demonstrates dangerous capabilities, making precautions responsive to evidence of risk.
